    Show, Don't Certify: How to Prepare for Your First Data Analyst Job

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
    • Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial.
    • It has been revealed that getting shortlisted for a junior data analyst job depends less on how many courses you have finished and more on what you can show.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

    Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

    It has been revealed that getting shortlisted for a junior data analyst job depends less on how many courses you have finished and more on what you can show. This plan breaks preparation into eight skill areas, pairs each one with a learning option and a hands-on task, and gives you a simple test for knowing when to move on.

    Many people preparing for their first analyst role study for months and still struggle to get interviews. Their CVs list SQL, Excel and Tableau, yet nothing on the page shows those tools being used to answer a real question. Recruiters reading dozens of similar applications need something more concrete.

    A course can give your learning a sensible order, but a completion badge says little about how you think. A small analysis that states its question, explains its method and admits its limits tells a hiring manager far more. This strategy aims to collect that kind of proof while you learn, not after.

    According to recent reports, start by collecting ten to twenty entry-level postings in the industry you want to join, and tally the tools and tasks they mention. You will rapidly see a pattern. Some roles are built around Excel and routine reporting, while others want SQL, a BI platform and a bit of Python.

    According to recent reports, the wider market follows a similar shape. Jobright’s 2026 analysis of data analyst hiring, which looked at 2025–2026 postings from LinkedIn, Indeed and Levels.fyi, found that more than 80% of data analyst jobs mention SQL, over 60% mention Excel or Google Sheets, and roughly half mention Python or R. Let your own tally decide the order you learn in, but expect SQL to sit near the top.

    Industry observers note that as you work through each area below, finish with something you can show someone: a query, a tidied dataset, a chart, a one-page report or a portfolio project. Free material is often enough if you can stay disciplined. Pay for teaching only when it gives you something you cannot get alone, such as feedback, accountability or a fixed timetable.

    In a recent development, SQL is how analysts pull, join and summarise records from a database, and a tool like Tableau lets other people explore what you found. Treat them as one workflow rather than two subjects: frame a question, write the query, sanity-check the numbers and present the result so a non-technical reader can follow it.

    SQLBolt offers free, bite-sized SQL lessons that run in the browser, and Tableau publishes free training videos on connecting to data and building dashboards. Used together, they are enough to produce a small end-to-end project.

    According to recent reports, if you learn better with a set schedule and an instructor checking your work, you could learn to analyse data with SQL and Tableau from scratch through a guided programme at Heicoders Academy in Singapore. Whichever route you take, compare what is covered, how feedback is given, when sessions run and the full cost against what free resources already offer.

    Proof you can show: A working SQL query set and your first published dashboard.

    Move on when: You can take a question from idea to dashboard on your own, without following a tutorial line by line.

    Recent findings suggest that spreadsheets are still where much of a team’s day-to-day reporting lives, especially when colleagues don’t write SQL. Get comfortable with filtering, pivot tables, and lookup functions, and learn to spot quiet errors like dates saved as text or one category spelled three different ways.

    Industry observers note that the next step is automating the cleanup so it doesn’t have to be repeated by hand each month. Microsoft’s Power Query documentation shows how to import and reshape data in recorded steps that refresh when new data arrives. The same ideas apply in other spreadsheet tools too.

    Proof you can show: A messy export turned into a summary that refreshes itself.

    Move on when: You can clean an untidy CSV and build a report that updates when the source file changes.

    For most junior analyst roles, the technical interview is a SQL test. Basic SELECT statements won’t be enough; interviewers like to probe joins, subqueries, common table expressions and window functions, which answer everyday questions such as running totals or each customer’s first purchase.

    Practise with timed problem sets and review your answers for correctness as well as speed.

    Proof you can show: Confidence going into a live or take-home SQL test.

    Move on when: You can solve intermediate problems in around 15 to 20 minutes each without looking up syntax.

    Take-home assignments often come with data that has been made messy on purpose. Reviewers want to see how you deal with missing values, duplicates and inconsistent formats, and whether they can follow your reasoning afterwards.

    Keep a short cleaning log as you work, noting each change and why you made it. A separate sheet tab or a list of comments in a notebook both work.

    Proof you can show: A take-home submission a reviewer can audit step by step.

    Move on when: Every change to your dataset is written down with a reason.

    In a recent development, case-study questions test whether you can read numbers sensibly, not just produce them. A working grasp of distributions, means and medians, spread, correlation and sampling will keep you away from the mistakes that undo otherwise good answers, such as quoting an average that a few extreme values have pulled out of shape.

    Proof you can show: Clear, careful answers in case-study interviews.

    Move on when: You can explain in everyday language why two things moving together doesn’t mean one causes the other.

    Every chart should help someone answer a specific question. Learn where bars, lines, scatter plots and simple tables each work best, and how axis ranges, labels and colour can nudge a reader towards the wrong conclusion. On a dashboard, the most crucial finding should be the first thing people see.

    Datawrapper’s guidance on picking chart types is a useful free reference. As practice, show the same result in two different chart types and decide which one represents the data more honestly.

    Proof you can show: Portfolio charts that make a point, not just show off features.

    Move on when: A person who has never seen your data can spot the main finding and its caveat at a glance.

    What counts as a useful metric depends on the role. Marketing analysts focus on conversion and retention, operations analysts on delivery times and capacity, and finance analysts on margins and cash flow. Choose one sector and learn exactly how its key measures are defined.

    Proof you can show: A project built around the questions your target industry actually asks.

    Move on when: You can define several sector metrics and describe how a manager would use each one.

    According to recent reports, your portfolio is where the other seven areas come together. Two or three deep, well-documented projects will say more about you than a long list of quick ones. Give each project a README that sets out the question, the data, your method, the findings and the limitations.

    Proof you can show: A portfolio link and a write-up you can talk through in an interview.

    Move on when: Every project clearly explains what it asked, how you answered it and what you found.

    It has been revealed that there is no need to finish all eight areas before you apply. Once you can use the tools your target roles mention, speak honestly about your work and point to two or three clearly explained projects, start sending applications and keep learning alongside them.

    Adjust each application to the job. Lead with a reporting example for spreadsheet-heavy roles, a query that solved a real problem for SQL roles, and a chart that supported a decision for visualisation roles. Be upfront about which work you built independently and which came from guided exercises.

    Do I really need eight courses? No. These are skill areas, not eight required qualifications. A single resource can cover several of them, and practice you do on your own counts as much as classroom learning.

    Is it possible to prepare using only free material? Yes. Free tutorials, open textbooks, official documentation and public datasets cover the fundamentals well. The harder parts are sticking to a routine and finding people who will give you honest feedback.

    According to recent reports, which should come first, SQL or spreadsheets? It depends on the jobs you want. Spreadsheets are an easy starting point for reporting roles, while SQL is expected wherever databases are involved. You will want both eventually, so start with whichever your target postings stress most.

    In a recent development, how many portfolio projects should I have? Two or three solid ones are a good start. Each should show a clear question, steps someone else could repeat and an honest reading of the results, rather than several near-identical dashboards.

    Industry observers note that do I need a certificate before I apply? Not usually. Some employers ask for one, but many judge skills through interviews, take-home tasks and tests instead. Go by what each posting actually requires.

    #115831. MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI

    📅 22 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1315 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

    MIT’s tiny flying robot gets 450% faster with AI

    📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes.
    • Until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them.
    • Researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a newly introduced approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tiny flying robots may one day help rescuers search for people trapped beneath collapsed buildings after earthquakes. Because of their small size, these robotic insects could potentially move through narrow spaces that larger drones cannot enter while avoiding walls, debris, and falling objects.

    Until recently, however, aerial microrobots have been far less nimble than the insects that inspired them. They typically moved slowly and followed relatively simple flight paths.

    Researchers at MIT have now demonstrated a newly introduced approach that gives an insect-scale flying robot much greater speed and agility. The team developed an AI-based controller that allows the robotic bug to perform demanding aerial maneuvers, including repeated body flips.

    Using a two-part control system designed to balance performance with computational efficiency, the researchers increased the robot's speed by about 450 percent and its acceleration by about 250 percent compared with their previous best results.

    The robot was agile enough to complete 10 consecutive somersaults in 11 seconds, even while wind disturbances tried to knock it away from its intended path.

    According to recent reports, "We want to be able to use these robots in scenarios that more traditional quadcopter robots would have trouble flying into, but that insects could navigate. Now, with our bioinspired control framework, the flight performance of our robot is comparable to insects in terms of speed, acceleration, and the pitching angle. This is quite an exciting step toward that future goal," says Kevin Chen, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), head of the Soft and Micro Robotics Laboratory within the Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), and co-senior author of a paper on the robot.

    Chen is joined on the paper by co-lead authors Yi-Hsuan Hsiao, an EECS MIT graduate student; Andrea Tagliabue PhD '24; and Owen Matteson, a graduate student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AeroAstro); as well as EECS graduate student Suhan Kim; Tong Zhao MEng '23; and co-senior author Jonathan P. How, the Ford Professor of Engineering in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and a principal investigator in the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS). The research was published in Science Advances.

    AI Gives the Robot a Smarter Flight Controller.

    Chen's group has spent more than five years developing robotic insects.

    According to recent reports, the team recently created a more durable version of their tiny robot, which is about the size of a microcassette and weighs less than a paperclip. This newer design has larger flapping wings that support more agile flight. The wings are driven by soft artificial muscles that contract rapidly enough to produce extremely fast wingbeats.

    The physical design had improved, but the robot's controller remained a major limitation. This controller acts as the robot's "brain," determining where the robot is and deciding how it should move. In earlier versions, a human had to tune the controller by hand.

    For the robot to fly with the speed and aggressiveness of a real insect, the researchers needed a system that could handle uncertainty while rapidly solving complex control problems.

    A controller powerful enough to do that would normally demand too much computation to operate in real time, especially because the aerodynamics of such a lightweight flying machine are highly complex.

    It has been revealed that to solve this problem, Chen's group collaborated with How's team to develop a two-step AI-driven control system. The design combines the robustness needed for difficult, high-speed maneuvers with enough computational efficiency to work in real time.

    "The hardware advances pushed the controller so there was more we could do on the software side, but at the same time, as the controller developed, there was more they could do with the hardware. As Kevin's team demonstrates fresh capabilities, we demonstrate that we can utilize them," How notes.

    Teaching a Tiny Robot to Plan Difficult Maneuvers.

    The first part of the system uses what is known as a model-predictive controller. This type of controller relies on a dynamic mathematical model to predict how the robot will behave and determine the best sequence of actions for safely following a desired flight path.

    Although this method requires substantial computing power, it can plan difficult movements such as aerial flips, sharp turns, and aggressive changes in body angle. The planner also takes into account limits on the amount of force and torque the robot can produce, helping it avoid movements that could lead to a crash.

    Repeated flips are particularly challenging. To perform one somersault after another, the robot must slow down in exactly the right way so that it begins each latest flip under the proper conditions.

    "If small errors creep in, and you try to repeat that flip 10 times with those small errors, the robot will just crash. We need to have robust flight control," How says.

    It has been revealed that the researchers then used this expert planner to train a "policy" built on a deep-learning model through a process called imitation learning. The policy serves as the robot's real-time decision-making system, determining how and where it should fly.

    In effect, imitation learning allows the team to capture the behavior of the more computationally demanding controller in a faster AI model that can operate quickly enough for real-time flight.

    A major part of the challenge was generating enough useful training data to teach the policy how to handle aggressive maneuvers without creating an unnecessarily large data set.

    "The robust training method is the secret sauce of this technique," How explains.

    During flight, the AI-based policy receives information about the robot's position and converts it into real-time commands controlling factors such as thrust force and torques.

    Industry observers note that experiments showed that the two-step control system dramatically improved the robot's performance. The insect-scale machine flew 447 percent faster and achieved a 255 percent increase in acceleration.

    It also completed 10 somersaults in only 11 seconds while remaining within about 4 or 5 centimeters of its planned flight path.

    "This work demonstrates that soft and microrobots, traditionally limited in speed, can now leverage advanced control algorithms to achieve agility approaching that of natural insects and larger robots, opening up upcoming opportunities for multimodal locomotion," states Hsiao.

    Sources indicate that the team also demonstrated a movement known as a saccade. In insects, this involves pitching the body sharply, rapidly moving to a newly introduced position, and then pitching in the opposite direction to stop. This quick acceleration and braking can help insects determine their position and maintain clear vision.

    "This bio-mimicking flight behavior could help us in the future when we start putting cameras and sensors on board the robot," Chen indicates.

    Toward Autonomous Flying Microrobots.

    Industry observers note that one major goal for future research is to equip the microrobots with onboard cameras and sensors. That could eventually allow them to fly outdoors without depending on a sophisticated external motion capture system.

    The team also aims to investigate whether onboard sensing could help groups of the robots avoid crashing into one another and coordinate their movements while navigating.

    "For the micro-robotics community, I hope this paper signals a paradigm shift by showing that we can develop a fresh control architecture that is high-performing and efficient at the same time," says Chen.

    This research is funded, in part, by the National Science Foundation (NSF), the Office of Naval Research, Air Force Office of Scientific Research, MathWorks, and the Zakhartchenko Fellowship.

    • Scientists were left stunned after finding a “surreal” site of kitchen appliances at the bottom of the ocean, all while they thought it was part of a shipwreck.
    • Oceans are, notoriously, one of the last places on Earth that haven’t been fully explored.
    • Back in 2017, a group of researchers from NOAA, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, had been using a ROV (remotely operated vehicle) in the Gulf of Mexico while looking for a shipwreck.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Scientists were left stunned after finding a “surreal” site of kitchen appliances at the bottom of the ocean, all while they thought it was part of a shipwreck.

    Oceans are, notoriously, one of the last places on Earth that haven’t been fully explored. The depths of some make it impossible for researchers to actually get a clear picture of what is lurking down there, even with all the money in the world being thrown behind some explorations.

    Back in 2017, a group of researchers from NOAA, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, had been using a ROV (remotely operated vehicle) in the Gulf of Mexico while looking for a shipwreck.

    However, instead of finding ancient treasure, they stumbled upon a field of kitchen appliances on the seafloor, and couldn’t quite believe it.

    In footage only released this year, almost a decade on, scientists from NOAA talked through their findings, with one expert calling it a “bit surreal” to see.

    “We are at 1.5km in the deep sea, and here we are moving through a field of chest freezers, fridges, and washing machines,” they added.

    Another joked that they’d “return this to the manufacturer and ask about the warranty,” when looking at one of the submerged washing machines.

    It has been revealed that the debris had been found as the researchers picked up a “sonar target,” which they suspected to be a shipwreck. Instead, they found a 40-foot-long shipping container with a hole on the outside of it. It is certainly a unique find.

    While the fridges and washing machines wouldn’t work on land, they had been put to work under the water, with the scientists finding coral growing on some, and fish also living around them.

    Elsewhere, in Italy, divers discovered a 3,300-year-old sword stuck under a lake, and it was in “excellent” condition with a sharp blade too.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Clicks is still on track to release the phone with a physical keyboard within the next few months, but a Communicator launch before the end of this year isn’t looking very likely as shipping gets pushed back.

    Industry observers note that the Communicator is a fresh take on what an Android phone can be. It was first introduced at CES earlier this year, with the main selling angle being the physically integrated keyboard. Clicks wants to target those who are looking for a second device, and the Communicator fits the bill.

    Recent findings suggest that last we heard, the Clicks Communicator was on track to launch and ship in December, following a cheery update detailing an upgrade to 12GB of RAM and other changes. However, Clicks posted a new update today stating that the timeline has shifted out a month because of supply chain issues caused by something other than RAM.

    Unfortunately, we’ve encountered a delay with securing a critical supply chain component needed to fabricate our printed circuit board ahead of manufacturing and final assembly. Assembly will now begin in early January, with deliveries expected to start in late January.

    It notes that the “critical supply chain component” is the essential fabric used for the firm’s printed circuit boards. The blog post dives into some neat details about the component holding things up. The PCBs Clicks is using are made up of more material layers than some competitor boards. But the fabric used to layer those boards is in short supply at this sort of demand, with four manufacturers reportedly unable to meet the company’s required volume.

    Recent findings suggest that the post also spells out difficulties caused by troubles in the Middle East, and rising memory costs straining the chain of supply further, even if memory – surprisingly – isn’t the cause of this small delay. Those compounded issues have pushed production back, and people are now told to expect their Clicks Communicator pre-orders to be shipped in late January, at the earliest. Many pre-orders will likely be shipped after that because of further time constraints before Chinese New Year.

    In an act of good faith, Clicks indicates it’s including a set of 3.5mm wired headphones in each box for orders placed prior to today.

    In a recent development, A push from December to January isn’t massive, and Clicks still seems to be making solid time on developing a form factor we don’t often see. You can still pre-order the Clicks Communicator starting at $649.

    • GTA 6’s launch has already drawn a reaction from CD Projekt Red, with Cyberpunk 2’s creative director joking that his own game was “cancelled” after seeing what Rockstar had pulled off.
    • However, the comparison came up again during CD Projekt’s earnings call, when the firm was asked whether players should expect a similar leap from its next Witcher game.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    CD Projekt Red states the jump from The Witcher 3 to The Witcher 4 will be comparable to the one Rockstar made between GTA 5 and GTA 6, with improvements planned for nearly every part of the game.

    GTA 6’s launch has already drawn a reaction from CD Projekt Red, with Cyberpunk 2’s creative director joking that his own game was “cancelled” after seeing what Rockstar had pulled off.

    However, the comparison came up again during CD Projekt’s earnings call, when the firm was asked whether players should expect a similar leap from its next Witcher game.

    As first reported by Eurogamer, CD Projekt Red co-CEO Michal Nowakowski said the studio had looked at what changed between Rockstar’s two games and that he expected The Witcher 4 to make a comparable jump.

    Industry observers note that “We believe there’s going to be a comparable leap between The Witcher 3 and The Witcher 4, I think so, yes. It’s been 11 years, we are working on The Witcher 4 to make it significantly better looking and improved in terms of pretty much every possible facet of the game, so yes, you should expect us to make a much bigger jump between Witcher 3 and Witcher 4,” mentioned Nowakowski.

    Industry observers note that nowakowski was also asked whether GTA 6’s launch would push CD Projekt Red to spend more on its own games. After all, GTA 6 is expected to have exceeded $1 billion in total development costs.

    However, the CD Projekt Red CEO remarked the studio’s ambitions for The Witcher 4 and Cyberpunk 2 had stayed the same.

    It has been revealed that “We have certain ambitions when it comes to Witcher [4] and Cyberpunk 2, they have not changed when it comes to GTA 6. If anything happened as a result of GTA 6, it’s [that it’s] always great to see games like that because they show you how much cool stuff can be done, and that’s for sure an inspiration in many ways for our developers,” he added.

    The Witcher 4 dev admits they are worried about living up to Witcher 3.

    CDPR boss hopes The Witcher 4 will win back fans after Cyberpunk 2077’s launch disaster.

    CD Projekt Red reveals major differences between Cyberpunk 2077 & Witcher 3.

    The Witcher 4 is being developed for PlayStation 5, PC, and Xbox Series X/S and is at the moment targeting a 2028 launch.

    Newly introduced CPU benchmark tool promises 40 years of compatibility, with support as far back as i386, Windows 95

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (462 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomshardware

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, there's a upcoming CPU benchmark on the way designed to handle and contextualize 40 years of personal computer chip development.
    • Windows 95/NT 3.51以降に対応し、i386から最新、さらに将来のCPUまで、 世代を超えて性能を一つの基準で評価する新世代CPUベンチマークソフト「CrystalMark CPUix」を鋭意企画中です。 CrystalMark CPUix Project Site https://t.co/OEjTdlr4bU https://t.co/ZAfjuz6sYtJuly 29, 2026.
    • In a recent development, miyazaki says that the upcoming CPUix app will support 16-color environments, which might help folks at the more ancient and creaky end of the PC retro hardware spectrum.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, there's a upcoming CPU benchmark on the way designed to handle and contextualize 40 years of personal computer chip development. The upcoming CrystalMark CPUix "evaluates performance from i386 through the latest processors using a single standard across past and future CPU generations," notes developer Noriyuki Miyazaki [machine translation]. In terms of hardware/software compatibility, the benchmarking tool will evaluate processors as old as the i386 running on OSes as out of date as Windows 95 and NT 3.51.

    Windows 95/NT 3.51以降に対応し、i386から最新、さらに将来のCPUまで、 世代を超えて性能を一つの基準で評価する新世代CPUベンチマークソフト「CrystalMark CPUix」を鋭意企画中です。 CrystalMark CPUix Project Site https://t.co/OEjTdlr4bU https://t.co/ZAfjuz6sYtJuly 29, 2026.

    In a recent development, miyazaki says that the upcoming CPUix app will support 16-color environments, which might help folks at the more ancient and creaky end of the PC retro hardware spectrum. Even this limited color UI will have a base maroon theme, as used in the announcement graphic.

    The developer is also welcoming feature requests on social media. Don't ask for support for OSes earlier than Windows 95, though, as it has already been stated by Miyazaki that stretching compatibility to Windows 3.1 "is a bit much.".

    To aid in the development of CPUix, Miyazaki has recently acquired an NEC PC-98 21Bs. This lovely beige desktop arrived on the developer's desk on Sunday, but it has already been used to implement and verify CPUix's functionality on processors without an FPU. Other older systems have been purchased, including a Pentium 100, to ensure wide compatibility. More systems, old and new, are also going to be acquired for testing.

    In a recent development, we don't have a lot of information on the inner workings of CPUix as yet. Aspects of the benchmark's test workloads, score weighting, and so on aren't shared on the official pages or social media postings we found. As CPUix comes from the developer of CrystalDiskMark, it looks like it could be a more ambitious version of the CrystalMark Retro 2.0.0 release, which we reported on last year. That also supported systems back to Windows 95/NT 3.51, and CPUs from the i386 era.

    According to recent reports, CPUix is still in development, and its release date is at the moment penciled in for March 31, 2027. It seems to have been revealed early, as Miyazaki celebrates the 28th anniversary of Crystal Dew World.

    #115823. Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal

    📅 25 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1176 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

    Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal

    📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software.
    • Sources indicate that scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons.
    • "We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," noted Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the latest study published in Nature.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software. Researchers have now demonstrated a new way to reach that level of flexibility using unusual quantum objects known as non-Abelian anyons.

    Sources indicate that scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons. Their results provide the first experimental demonstration that this approach can support the broad range of operations required for universal quantum computing.

    "We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," noted Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the latest study published in Nature.

    A Possible Shortcut Around Costly Quantum Error Correction.

    The strategy could do more than help create a general-purpose quantum computer. It may also offer a more efficient route toward reliable quantum machines.

    Industry observers note that quantum computers are extremely vulnerable to errors, so researchers typically protect information by distributing it across many physical qubits. These error correction methods can preserve data, but they usually do not provide every operation needed to perform universal quantum computation on that protected information.

    It has been revealed that to fill the gap, engineers often rely on specially prepared resources called "magic states." Producing them usually requires an intensive purification process known as distillation, which can consume a large fraction of a quantum computer's available qubits. The fresh results suggest that non-Abelian anyons may offer a way around that expensive step.

    "Non-Abelian codes are a dark horse in the race to quantum error correction," said Henrik Dreyer, managing director and scientific lead at Quantinuum's Munich office and a co-author of the study. "In this work we show the first universal gate set in a non-Abelian code, which demonstrates that fault-tolerant computations can in principle be done without resorting to magic state distillation or cultivation, which are the most expensive operations in standard quantum error correction codes.".

    Why Non-Abelian Anyons Are Different.

    Ordinary qubits encode information using two basic states, along with quantum combinations of those states. Non-Abelian anyons work in a fundamentally different way.

    These anyons do not appear as ordinary standalone particles in nature. Instead, scientists create them inside quantum circuits by entangling many conventional qubits into a collective state that behaves as though it were a upcoming type of particle with its own unusual rules.

    "The way I think about these codes is they're creating little universes -- alternative universes, but ones that reflect some of the properties of our own," Verresen stated.

    Each non-Abelian anyon carries an internal state that changes when one anyon is moved around another in a process known as braiding. The sequence of those braiding operations matters (that's what non-Abelian means), allowing information to be encoded and manipulated in ways that are unavailable to ordinary particles.

    Because the information is spread across many entangled qubits rather than stored in a single location, it can also be naturally protected from some of the small disturbances that frequently disrupt conventional qubits. Braiding the anyons can also perform computational operations.

    Why Braiding Alone Was Not Enough.

    In 2024, a research team that included Verresen used a Quantinuum trapped-ion computer to create anyons associated with a symmetry group called D4 -- the rotations and reflections that leave a square unchanged -- demonstrating this form of non-Abelian order on quantum hardware for the first time.

    That experiment highlighted that the unusual particles could be created and manipulated, but braiding them alone was not sufficient to carry out every operation required for universal quantum computing.

    Sources indicate that "In that work, we didn't demonstrate that those emergent forces were enough to do quantum computation," mentioned Verresen. "That particular universe we created was not powerful enough.".

    Fusion Unlocks Universal Quantum Operations.

    For the new study, the researchers switched to another symmetry known as S3 -- the rotations and mirror-image flips that leave an equilateral triangle unchanged -- and created the corresponding anyons on Quantinuum's H2 trapped-ion processor using 54 entangled qubits.

    The S3 system had the properties needed for universal quantum computation, but only when braiding was combined with another operation called fusion. During fusion, two anyons are brought together and the resulting state is measured.

    The underlying concept was proposed theoretically in 2003 by Carlos Mochon, then a student of John Preskill at Caltech. Turning that theoretical idea into an experiment that could actually run on quantum hardware, however, required extensive additional theoretical and experimental work.

    The researchers used pairs of anyons to encode "topological qutrits" which store three possible levels of quantum information instead of the two levels used by ordinary qubits.

    Recent findings suggest that by combining different braiding and fusion operations, the team demonstrated three key tools: one entangling gate produced through braiding and two different measurements created through fusion. Together, those operations can in principle produce any quantum operation, including operations that braiding alone could not achieve.

    Beyond their possible computing applications, these unusual quantum states could also help researchers investigate fundamental aspects of physics.

    "It is gratifying to see ideas we have spent our PhD work thinking about realized in the lab, and it has been made possible by remarkable advances in quantum hardware over the past few years," remarked Anasuya Lyons and Chiu Fan Bowen Lo, graduate students at Harvard University in the group of Ashvin Vishwanath who helped lead the work.

    Toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers.

    The researchers also demonstrated that non-Abelian anyons could directly produce a magic state using topological operations -- sidestepping the costly distillation process used in most quantum systems.

    In a recent development, the experiment did not yet include active error correction. Instead, the researchers focused on testing the individual building blocks of the method and confirming that they could create a magic state consistent with theoretical expectations.

    Recent findings suggest that "So far, we've ignored the question of error correction. Here, it's more like a proof of principle," Verresen said.

    The next major step will be combining these operations with active error correction. If that can be achieved, non-Abelian anyons could eventually become a practical basis for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers. Verresen is already working with other PME researchers on fresh techniques for stabilizing non-Abelian quantum memories.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Formula 1 world champion Max Verstappen revealed he played 40 hours of Grand Theft Auto 6 ahead of his win at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.
    • It has been revealed that on November 19, after 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto fans were finally able to jump into GTA 6.
    • The release also disrupted the world of sports, too.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Formula 1 world champion Max Verstappen revealed he played 40 hours of Grand Theft Auto 6 ahead of his win at the Las Vegas Grand Prix.

    It has been revealed that on November 19, after 13 years of waiting, Grand Theft Auto fans were finally able to jump into GTA 6. Rockstar Games’ long-awaited release disrupted the global economy, with millions of fans taking at least one day off to get stuck into the latest game.

    The release also disrupted the world of sports, too. Formula One legend Lewis Hamilton revealed he was hoping to take the day off to play it, while NBA star Steven Adams said that sports leagues would “plummet” in quality as a result of GTA 6.

    In the case of Max Verstappen, the Dutch F1 star is a keen gamer and regularly streams on Twitch between races. He had spoken about wanting to play GTA 6 upon release beforehand, and has finally revealed how he went about it.

    According to recent reports, “I played a lot in the evening and in the morning in Vegas,” the four-time F1 world champion explained. “I mean, I can’t go out anyways and walk around.”.

    Verstappen added that he didn’t play on his flight back from Las Vegas, choosing to catch up on some sleep instead.

    According to recent reports, while he often dips in and out of games – including ARC Raiders and sim racing – he can’t juggle playing too many at once. “I’m so bad when I play too many games at the same time. I can’t, I just can’t,” he added.

    🤯Max Verstappen played GTA VI for FORTY HOURS while in Las VegasOn top of that, he also won the race pic.twitter.com/jwuxQnHxyS.

    The 40 hours of gameplay came as he went on to win the Vegas Grand Prix as well, securing his fourth victory of the season.

    The Red Bull Racing driver might drive one of the fastest cars in real life, but there are plenty for you to find across Leonida.

    On top of that, cheat codes have made a return in GTA 6, but you will have to play through Jason and Lucia’s story to unlock quite a few of them.

    #115820. Industry News: This light-powered AI can spot deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy

    📅 01 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1096 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: This light-powered AI can spot deepfakes with nearly 98% accuracy

    📅 01 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1096 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) have created a upcoming optical-neural processor that uses light to help identify deepfake videos rapidly and accurately.
    • The key difference is that part of the detection process takes place through the physical propagation of light.
    • The technology is detailed in the study "Scalable, Energy-Efficient Optical-Neural Architecture for Multiplexed Deepfake Video Detection," published in eLight.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) have created a upcoming optical-neural processor that uses light to help identify deepfake videos rapidly and accurately. Unlike conventional systems that typically examine videos one after another using digital hardware, the UCLA technology can analyze 15 or more video streams at the same time.

    The key difference is that part of the detection process takes place through the physical propagation of light. This allows many videos to be evaluated simultaneously during a single optical pass rather than requiring each one to move separately through a conventional digital processing pipeline.

    The technology is detailed in the study "Scalable, Energy-Efficient Optical-Neural Architecture for Multiplexed Deepfake Video Detection," published in eLight. The researchers designed the optical AI system to serve as a high-throughput, attack-resilient first layer of defense for screening large amounts of manipulated and AI-generated video.

    The Growing Challenge of Deepfake Detection.

    Rapid improvements in generative AI have made synthetic videos increasingly realistic, increasing the need for detection systems that are both accurate and capable of operating at large scale.

    Many advanced deepfake detectors depend on enormous amounts of digital computation. A single analysis can require hundreds of billions of floating-point operations, and videos are often processed sequentially. As more content must be checked, both the processing time and energy requirements can rise proportionally.

    Digital detection systems face another problem. Attackers can deliberately alter fake videos in subtle ways designed to confuse a detector and make manipulated footage appear authentic.

    Professor Aydogan Ozcan and his UCLA team developed a hybrid digital-optical system intended to address both challenges.

    A lightweight digital encoder first collects compact information about each video, including spatial, spectral, and temporal features. That information is transformed into a phase pattern and displayed on a programmable spatial light modulator.

    The resulting optical wavefront then travels through a free-space-based, passive optical decoder. At the other end, paired optical detectors directly produce an authenticity score for each video.

    In effect, the system replaces a computationally demanding digital decoding network with a physical process that can handle many streams in parallel.

    Nearly 98% Accuracy Across 15 Videos at Once.

    In experiments using visible light, the processor examined 15 Celeb-DF videos simultaneously during each optical pass.

    It has been revealed that it achieved an average detection accuracy of 97.79%, along with a sensitivity of 99.86% and a specificity of 95.72%. Sensitivity measures how successfully the system identifies manipulated videos, making the particularly high sensitivity vital for a screening tool designed to keep fake content from slipping through.

    The 99.86% sensitivity translated to an average false-negative rate of ~0.14%. In other words, only a very small fraction of manipulated videos were incorrectly classified as authentic.

    The researchers also pushed the system further by increasing its capacity to 18 videos in a single optical pass. Even at that level, average detection accuracy remained at 96.13%.

    More Optical Layers Boost Performance.

    The team found that the processor could also become more capable by increasing the physical depth of its passive optical decoder without substantially increasing energy use or inference latency.

    When researchers added two optimized passive diffractive layers while testing more difficult deepfake manipulations, detection accuracy improved by ~6.8%.

    These phase-only diffractive layers can be manufactured as passive, static optical structures/surfaces. They perform additional calculations through the diffraction of light, meaning they do not require additional electrical power while the system is performing an inference.

    That approach could allow more sophisticated processing without the same energy costs that typically accompany larger digital neural networks.

    Testing the System Against Google VEO-3 Videos.

    The researchers did not limit their experiments to conventional face swapping deepfakes. They also challenged the processor with videos produced using Google's VEO-3 model.

    Newer generative AI systems can create footage that lacks many of the obvious artifacts associated with earlier deepfake technology, making them a more difficult target for detectors trained primarily on older forms of manipulation.

    With only minimal fine-tuning, the optical processor achieved 94.80% accuracy and 97.61% sensitivity on previously unseen VEO-3 videos during experiments.

    The results suggest that the approach could potentially adapt as generative AI technology continues to evolve.

    A Deepfake Detector Designed to Be Harder to Fool.

    The optical system also indicated resistance to black-box adversarial attacks and provides inherent protection against white-box attacks.

    Part of that security comes from the way the detector physically performs its calculations. Because some of the inference process takes place through diffraction, notable parameters of the optical model are effectively embedded within the hardware.

    Recent findings suggest that those parameters can be difficult for an attacker to measure, reproduce, or reverse engineer. That makes reconstructing the detector and designing carefully tailored adversarial changes that can evade it considerably more difficult.

    Industry observers note that the processor also continued working reliably when videos were affected by image noise, blur, JPEG compression, and experimental misalignments. According to the researchers, those results illustrate how optical computation could provide a more secure and dependable foundation for some artificial intelligence systems.

    A First Line of Defense Against Deepfakes.

    Rather than replacing sophisticated digital detectors entirely, the UCLA processor is designed to work as a highly sensitive first stage of a larger detection system.

    Massive volumes of video could initially pass through the parallel optical processor. Content identified as suspicious could then be sent to more computationally demanding digital models for a more detailed final assessment.

    It has been revealed that such a system could combine the strengths of both approaches. Optical processing could provide parallel operation, low decoder energy requirements, high sensitivity, resistance to adversarial attacks, and the ability to adapt to newer AI video generators, while conventional digital systems could provide deeper analysis when necessary.

    The researchers say this combination could eventually be useful for large-scale content moderation, media authentication, surveillance, and other security-critical AI applications.

    The authors of this work are Parnian Ghapandar Kashani and Dr. Shiqi Chen, who contributed equally, and Professor Aydogan Ozcan. The researchers are affiliated with the UCLA Electrical and Computer Engineering Department, the UCLA Bioengineering Department, and the California NanoSystems Institute.

    Industry observers note that materials provided by Light Publishing Center, Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics And Physics, CAS. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

    Industry News: What Is the Best UI design Tool? 8 Tools Compared by the Job They Do (2026)

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
    • Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial.
    • Industry observers note that the ideal UI testing tool is the one that discovers what your customers discover first: broken layouts, usability concerns that no longer work, and new accessibility issues in all the browsers your users use before a change goes into the repository.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

    Sources indicate that weekly. Free. One click to leave.

    Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

    Industry observers note that the ideal UI testing tool is the one that discovers what your customers discover first: broken layouts, usability concerns that no longer work, and new accessibility issues in all the browsers your users use before a change goes into the repository. In 2026, most frontend teams don't rely on a single tool to do all of that. The best setups involve two layers: a test runner layer that releases the browser and monitors behavior, and a UI testing and review platform that visually checks the outcome and routes changes to the right stakeholders for sign-off.

    It has been revealed that even with the right stack, it still relies on what your team needs to catch. Different teams will focus on different points: a QA team trying to automate checkout flows, a design system team defending shared components, and a single developer working on a tight budget will all be somewhere different. This guide is categorized by the job these UI testing tools do, then connects them.

    It has been revealed that most "best UI testing tool" lists rank test runners and visual testing platforms against each other as if they were interchangeable. They aren't. UI testing covers four distinct jobs:.

    Functional testing: Does the UI respond correctly when a user clicks, types, or hovers?

    Visual testing: Does the UI still look right across layout, color, typography, and spacing?

    Accessibility testing: Can people using keyboards and screen readers use it, and did this change introduce newly introduced violations?

    Cross-browser and device coverage: Does it work in Safari on mobile, not just Chrome on a developer's laptop?

    There are also other levels of UI tests. Unit tests test the logic but don't interact with the UI. End-to-end (E2E) tests represent the full user journey in a browser but are difficult to set up, hard to troubleshoot when the bug is a visual detail, and can't practically test every state. Between the extremes of unit tests and E2E tests, component tests simulate each component's behavior in a real browser using fixed inputs, offering speed closer to unit tests and user-level coverage closer to E2E. Many teams maintain a thin layer of E2E tests for critical journeys, and they have component tests for the dozens of states a component may be in.

    These tools are organized by job so you can stack them rather than choose one winner.

    These platforms sit on top of your test runner. They capture rendered UI, compare it to approved baselines, and give your team a place to review what changed.

    Industry observers note that chromatic is a UI testing and review platform made by the Storybook team. It catches visual, interaction, and accessibility bugs in components and pages before they merge, and it gives developers, designers, and product managers one place to review UI changes and sign off. Chromatic's team is the core maintainer of Storybook, which has about 90,000 GitHub stars and 17 million weekly npm downloads, and a Vitest core maintainer on the team built Chromatic's Vitest integration. Chromatic is used by 45 Fortune 100 companies, including GitHub, Shopify, Microsoft, Adobe, the BBC, and monday.com.

    Industry observers note that pricing: Free initiative with 5,000 snapshots per month (Chrome only), unlimited projects and users. Starter is $179/month for 35,000 snapshots and adds Safari, Firefox, and Edge. Pro is $399/month for 85,000 snapshots. Enterprise is custom, with SSO, SCIM, SLA support, and data retention. TurboSnap snapshots count as 0.2 of a regular snapshot.

    Sources indicate that trade-offs: Chromatic is strongest when your UI is built from components. Teams with no component tests can start from Playwright or Cypress E2E tests, but they'll get the most value once components are covered too. Snapshot usage also grows with each browser and viewport you add, so strategy coverage before you scale it.

    Best for: Design system teams, product teams that want designers and PMs to approve UI changes, React Native teams, and Vitest-first teams that want visual testing without baselines stored in the repo.

    In a recent development, percy is BrowserStack's visual testing platform. It captures screenshots from your existing tests, renders them across browsers and responsive widths, and highlights pixel differences for review.

    Industry observers note that strengths: Framework-agnostic SDKs for Playwright, Cypress, Selenium, and Storybook. App Percy covers native mobile apps. The free plan includes 5,000 screenshots per month with unlimited people and projects.

    Sources indicate that trade-offs: Percy is page-oriented, and each page rendered in each browser at each width counts as a separate screenshot, so usage climbs promptly with cross-browser coverage. Percy compares feature branches against a base branch, which teams with complex branching should test early. Reviewers see rendered screenshots rather than an inspectable copy of the code under test, so debugging a diff usually means reproducing it locally.

    Pricing: Free tier, then paid looks with fixed screenshot allowances and overage.

    Best for: Teams already paying for BrowserStack that want visual checks on page-level E2E tests.

    Sources indicate that applitools Eyes uses Visual AI to compare screenshots the way a person would, with match levels that can ignore content changes and focus on layout. Its Ultrafast Grid re-renders captured page states across many browser, viewport, and device combinations.

    Strengths: Mature AI matching, broad browser and device coverage, Figma and Storybook testing, accessibility testing, and an MCP server. Higher tiers add AI-driven functional testing and plain-English test authoring.

    It has been revealed that trade-offs: Applitools is priced and packaged for enterprises. There's a free trial but no free plan, and the Starter plan is $667/month billed annually for 100,000 component checkpoints or 1,000 page checkpoints. Professional and Enterprise are custom-priced.

    Best for: Large QA organizations with major cross-browser matrices and budget for a dedicated visual AI platform.

    It has been revealed that backstopJS is a free, open-source visual regression testing tool released under the MIT license. You list the URLs, viewports, and CSS selectors to capture in a config file, and BackstopJS renders them in a headless browser through Playwright or Puppeteer, then compares the results against approved reference screenshots. The core workflow runs on three commands: backstop init, backstop test, and backstop approve.

    Industry observers note that strengths: Completely free, with no screenshot limits. A built-in browser report shows reference and test images side by side with a visual diff inspector, and changes can be approved from there. Optional Docker rendering keeps screenshots consistent between laptops and CI; Playwright adds Firefox and WebKit, and click, hover, and keypress selectors capture interactive states. JUnit reports plug into existing CI pipelines.

    Trade-offs: BackstopJS is self-hosted, so there's no cloud dashboard, shared team review, or pull request status checks out of the box. Reference screenshots are usually committed to your repository, and every page or component state you want to test needs its own URL and scenario in the config. Someone on the team also has to own the setup, CI integration, and maintenance.

    Best for: Developers and small teams with no budget who are comfortable running and maintaining their own visual regression setup.

    Industry observers note that test runners click, type, and assert. They're free and open source, and every platform above builds on them. On their own, they offer limited visual testing: built-in screenshot assertions store baselines in your repository, rendering can drift between laptops and CI, and designers have no review interface.

    Recent findings suggest that playwright is Microsoft's open-source browser automation framework. It runs tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, with auto-waiting, trace viewer debugging and code generation, and supports JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.

    Visual testing: Playwright's toHaveScreenshot assertion compares screenshots against baselines stored in Git. It works, but baselines must be regenerated per operating system, and accepting a change means rerunning with an update flag.

    In a recent development, best for: Teams automating critical user journeys such as sign-up, checkout and login. Pair it with a platform like Chromatic for visual review across real browsers.

    Industry observers note that cypress is an open-source testing tool that runs inside the browser, with time-travel debugging that indicates the app at each step of a test. It supports both E2E and component testing.

    Visual testing: Cypress has no built-in visual comparison and relies on plugins or a platform such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools. Cypress Cloud, its paid service, adds recording, parallelization, flake detection and add-ons for accessibility and UI coverage.

    Best for: Frontend developers who want fast feedback and an interactive test runner while they build.

    Storybook is the open source workshop for building UI components in isolation. Each story captures one component state, and those stories double as test cases.

    Testing features: Interaction tests with play functions and Testing Library, accessibility checks with the a11y addon, and a Vitest integration that runs stories as component tests.

    Visual testing: Storybook doesn't diff screenshots on its own. Chromatic, built by the same team, is its visual testing and review layer.

    Best for: Design system and component library teams, and any team practicing component-driven development.

    Vitest Browser Mode runs component tests in a real browser instead of a simulated DOM, using Playwright or WebdriverIO under the hood.

    It has been revealed that visual testing: Vitest's toMatchScreenshot assertion stores screenshots in the repository. For large projects, this can bloat the repo and baselines drift between machines. Chromatic can take Vitest Browser Mode tests with no code changes and run them in a stable cloud environment instead.

    Best for: Teams already writing Vitest tests who want them to check how the UI looks without adopting a upcoming framework.

    Start from the problem your team is trying to fix:.

    "Shared component changes keep breaking other teams' screens." Test at the component level with Storybook or Vitest Browser Mode and Chromatic, so the change reveals up on the pull request that caused it.

    According to recent reports, "Our Playwright tests pass, but the layout still breaks in Safari." Functional assertions don't check appearance. Add a visual testing platform that renders in Safari, such as Chromatic, Percy or Applitools.

    "We turned off screenshot tests because of false alarms." Look for deterministic component states and flake controls such as Chromatic's SteadySnap, or AI matching such as Applitools.

    "Designers find UI bugs after release." Choose a platform with a review and approval workflow, and make sign-off a required pull request check.

    "AI coding agents keep inventing components." Give agents access to your real component library, for example through Chromatic's hosted MCP, and run every agent-built change through the same UI tests as human code.

    "We have no budget." Use Playwright or Vitest screenshot assertions, self-host BackstopJS, or start on the free tiers of Chromatic or Percy.

    A practical, well-covered setup for a React web app looks like this:.

    Unit tests in Vitest for logic and utilities.

    Storybook stories or Vitest Browser Mode tests for every meaningful component state, with interaction tests on key components.

    Chromatic running visual, interaction and accessibility tests on those components in Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge on every pull request, with designers assigned as reviewers.

    A thin layer of Playwright E2E tests for sign-up, checkout and other critical journeys, also captured in Chromatic so page-level visual changes go through the same review.

    This keeps most UI coverage in fast, deterministic component tests, while E2E tests confirm the journeys that matter most still work end to end.

    Playwright is the best free tool for E2E UI testing, and Storybook is the best free tool for testing component states. For visual testing, For visual testing, Chromatic and Percy both offer free tiers of around 5,000 snapshots or screenshots per month, and BackstopJS is free to self-host.

    UI testing is the broad practice of checking that an interface works for users, including functional, visual and accessibility checks. Visual testing is one part of it: comparing rendered UI against approved baselines to catch unintended changes in layout, color, typography and spacing.

    According to recent reports, no. Chromatic was built by the Storybook team, but it also runs visual tests from Vitest Browser Mode, Playwright and Cypress tests, and from React Native Storybook on iOS and Android simulators.

    Playwright's toHaveScreenshot covers basic visual checks, but baselines live in your repo, rendering can differ between machines, and there's no review interface for designers. Teams with several reviewers or many browsers usually add a platform on top.

    Most teams use both. Component tests cover individual UI states rapidly and reliably, while a smaller set of E2E tests confirms that critical user journeys work across the whole app.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • GTA 6 players who used the New Zealand trick to play early on PS5 may have inadvertently purchased a censored version of the game that’s missing a useful stamina buff.
    • With GTA 6 launching at midnight local time on November 19, impatient fans around the world used the Upcoming Zealand trick to get a head start on their adventures in Leonida.
    • While Xbox players could simply change their console’s location, PS5 owners had to create a New Zealand PlayStation account and purchase GTA 6 through the country’s digital storefront.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    GTA 6 players who used the New Zealand trick to play early on PS5 may have inadvertently purchased a censored version of the game that’s missing a useful stamina buff.

    With GTA 6 launching at midnight local time on November 19, impatient fans around the world used the Upcoming Zealand trick to get a head start on their adventures in Leonida.

    While Xbox players could simply change their console’s location, PS5 owners had to create a New Zealand PlayStation account and purchase GTA 6 through the country’s digital storefront.

    Unfortunately, getting into Vice City a few hours early appears to have come with an unexpected drawback.

    As reported by IGN, Rockstar left out the ability to consume cocaine from your inventory in the Australian version of GTA 6, with Latest Zealand reportedly receiving the same version.

    Industry observers note that in the international release, players can collect baggies of cocaine or skim some off larger bricks. Consuming cocaine through the item wheel gives players a supercharged stamina bar for roughly 30 seconds.

    Australia’s video game classification rules allow depictions of illicit drug use but prohibit players from receiving gameplay benefits for taking them, even in games rated R18+.

    Interestingly, Upcoming Zealand doesn’t have this same restriction, but testing by GTA BOOM found that the mechanic was also absent from its New Zealand playthroughs.

    Players had already suspected GTA 6 was censored in certain regions before launch when dataminers discovered a roughly 700KB discrepancy in the Australian and New Zealand game files.

    Unlike Xbox consumers who temporarily changed their console’s location, PS5 players who bought the Newly introduced Zealand edition still own that regional copy even when playing on their regular account.

    Industry observers note that luckily, those affected aren’t missing out on too much. Adrenaline can still be used to boost stamina and other stats, while scripted sequences involving cocaine remain intact.

    Still, it’s a rather amusing twist that some of GTA 6‘s most impatient fans ended up with less content than those who waited a few extra hours.

    This newly introduced qubit could be 100 times less error-prone in superfluid quantum computer breakthrough

    📅 01 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (785 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Researchers at the University of Surrey have proposed a newly introduced kind of qubit that could help address one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing: keeping error rates low as systems become larger.
    • The concept uses superfluid helium, a form of helium with unusual quantum properties, to create a qubit that may be less sensitive to some of the disturbances that affect today's leading quantum computers.
    • It has been revealed that quantum computers rely on qubits to store and process information in ways that conventional computers cannot.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Researchers at the University of Surrey have proposed a newly introduced kind of qubit that could help address one of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing: keeping error rates low as systems become larger.

    The concept uses superfluid helium, a form of helium with unusual quantum properties, to create a qubit that may be less sensitive to some of the disturbances that affect today's leading quantum computers.

    Why Quantum Computers Struggle With Errors.

    It has been revealed that quantum computers rely on qubits to store and process information in ways that conventional computers cannot. Many current systems use superconducting circuits, but these are highly sensitive to electromagnetic noise and stray electrical charges - similar to the static electricity that can make hair cling to a balloon.

    It has been revealed that even very small disturbances can disrupt the fragile quantum information stored in a qubit. As more qubits are added, controlling those errors becomes increasingly difficult, making scalability one of the central challenges in quantum computing.

    In a study published in npj Quantum Information, researchers from Surrey's Quantum Sciences Group describe a different approach built around superfluid helium-3 - an unusual form of liquid helium that can flow without friction.

    According to recent reports, their proposed device, called the Superfluid Helium Oscillator Quantum (SHOQ) device, would use charge-neutral superfluid helium. Because the helium carries no electric charge, the design could be naturally protected from certain types of electromagnetic noise.

    A Qubit With Much Lower Predicted Error Rates.

    According to the researchers, this is the first reported design for a qubit based on a superfluid. Their calculations suggest the SHOQ device could have error rates about 100 times lower than conventional superconducting qubits.

    Dr. Priya Sharma, Daphne Jackson Fellow in Hybrid Quantum Systems at the University of Surrey's School of Mathematics and Physics, and lead author of the study, mentioned:.

    "We are not the first to think about the individual components behind this idea, but what we have done for the first time is bring them together in a microfluidic device and work out the specific details that could enable the device to function as a qubit.

    Sources indicate that "The maths tells us that it should work. We have taken what we already know about superfluid helium and quantum technologies and turned that into an educated design, with the parameters and specifications needed to build one. The next step is to make a prototype and put those predictions to the test.".

    Rather than replacing existing quantum computing hardware, the researchers say the SHOQ device could potentially be integrated with superconducting quantum technology.

    That could allow different types of qubits to perform different jobs within the same system, depending on their strengths.

    A Possible Role as Quantum Memory.

    One longer-term possibility is to use the SHOQ device as a form of quantum memory. In that setup, a superfluid based qubit could store quantum information while other hardware carries out calculations.

    According to recent reports, dr. Eran Ginossar, Associate Professor at the University of Surrey's Department of Physics and Advanced Technology Institute, and co-author of the study, said:.

    In a recent development, "We don't necessarily need one type of qubit to do everything. Combining different quantum technologies could allow us to take advantage of the strengths of each.

    "Superfluid helium gives us a fundamentally different type of quantum hardware to explore. If the predicted performance can be demonstrated experimentally, it could eventually work alongside existing superconducting technologies as part of a larger quantum system.".

    The Next Step Is Building a Prototype.

    Industry observers note that the team now looks to build a prototype to find out whether the predicted performance can be reproduced in a real device. That effort is being supported by an IAA Commercialisation Fellowship awarded to Dr. Priya Sharma.

    The SHOQ device would need to operate at extremely low temperatures, but researchers have already reached the necessary conditions in previous experiments involving superfluid helium-3.

    In a recent development, the project was led by the University of Surrey in collaboration with Professor Jens Koch at Northwestern University in the United States. Koch was one of the researchers involved in developing the transmon - a superconducting qubit design that is now widely used in quantum computing.

    Industry observers note that materials provided by University of Surrey. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

    • Quite literally at the start of this week, I was on a walk through my neighborhood and though to myself, “it’s still pretty annoying that I can’t see my workout progress in the Google Health app.” It’s been a complaint of mine for a while, as various treadmill sessions and more have left me wondering what my heart rate is looking like, how many steps I’ve taken, etc, and it’s only a problem when using the Fitbit Air, seeing as the Pixel Watch (or Fitbit Edge) I’d wear otherwise will show that data front and center.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google’s Fitbit Air is one of my favorite products of 2026 and my preferred workout companion, but not being able to see a workout while you’re in the middle of it has been a huge complaint of mine, and the latest Google Health enhancement is fixing that.

    Quite literally at the start of this week, I was on a walk through my neighborhood and though to myself, “it’s still pretty annoying that I can’t see my workout progress in the Google Health app.” It’s been a complaint of mine for a while, as various treadmill sessions and more have left me wondering what my heart rate is looking like, how many steps I’ve taken, etc, and it’s only a problem when using the Fitbit Air, seeing as the Pixel Watch (or Fitbit Edge) I’d wear otherwise will show that data front and center.

    Google Health 5.13 is fixing that.

    In the changelog for Google Health 5.13, Google details a new “exercise in-progress” card on the main “Today” screen. This will show what exercise is being tracked and also let you end the workout early.

    Industry observers note that if you use your Pixel Watch, Fitbit Air, or Fitbit Edge to automatically track your exercises, you’ll now see an exercise-in-progress card on your mobile app’s Today screen. This card lets you know that your device is tracking your exercise and gives you the opportunity to end the tracking and get your summary whenever you want.

    We don’t know exactly what this card looks like just yet, but it sounds like it fits the need perfectly.

    Google Health 5.13 is now rolling out on Android and iOS.
